title: KEDA sensitivity ramp + warm-pool cohorting — post-incident investigation and remediation
creator: Ava Patel
description: During a regional capacity event on 2026-02-18 we observed a series of rapid KEDA-driven scale ups followed by synchronous scale downs that caused elevated cold-start latency for a subset of critical serving pods. Investigation showed an interaction between a recent KEDA sensitivity change, warm-pool bucketization logic, and noisy probe signals that amplified false-positive scale decisions for low-latency lanes.
impact_summary: For ~23 minutes, 4% of production requests to the small-sequence text-generation tier experienced tail latency spikes (99th percentile increased from 120ms to ~1.8s). Internal throttles and retry traffic exacerbated the load on GPU pools resulting in temporary SLA breaches for a handful of customers. No data loss or tenant crossover occurred.

2026-02-18 09:26 UTC - Traffic normalized after warm-pool rehydration completed and hysteresis applied

detection: Alerting via autoscale-churn rule (rate of pod create/delete > 6 in 5 min) and customer-reported latency dashboards. Initial detection was noisy due to probe flapping; root detection relied on cross-correlation of KEDA trigger counts and per-pod readiness probe failure spikes.
root_cause: A recent KEDA sensitivity change (commit runtime:feat/keda-sensitivity-ramp) introduced a faster ramp for scaler trigger thresholds. Combined with warm-pool cohorting that groups small-latency customers into a narrow bucket, probe noise (TCP half-open spikes during brief network blips) produced transient trigger surges. KEDA reacted to these surges before the warm-pool fully rehydrated, leading to overshoot and then synchronous scale-down when several pods reported readiness at once.
contributing_factors: 1) Aggressive sensitivity ramping without percentile-smoothing for noisy signals. 2) Warm-pool bucketization reduced diversity of probe timing within a cohort. 3) Lack of a short-term hysteresis/clamp on scale-down decisions. 4) Insufficient telemetry surfaced to KEDA for per-model tail latency (we only fed average latency).
mitigation_taken:
- Immediately rolled back the sensitivity ramp change for the affected clusters (rollback tag runtime@2026-02-17).
- Applied a temporary scale-down inhibit (120s) on the small-sequence warm-pools to avoid synchronized downsizing.
- Enabled a conservative fallback route to the slower model variant for the busiest customer lanes during remediation.
action_items: PR: Implement percentile-based input for KEDA triggers (99th/95th) instead of mean - runtime PR #8132
Config: Add a sigmoid ramp function for KEDA sensitivity to smooth transient spikes - deploy config change to staging by 2026-03-05
Config: Increase minimum scale-down cooloff for warm-pool cohorts from 30s to 120s and add per-cohort jitter - runtime-1.22 rollout
Feature: Warm-pool cohort bucketization: add diversity window so cohorts are sampled across request phases (reduce synchronous readiness) - spec in Confluence
Telemetry: Surface per-model 99th latency into autoscaling pipeline and add KEDA input metric exporter - Grafana dashboard and alert updates
Tests: Add chaos test in staging that simulates network blips and probe flapping to validate hysteresis - cycle 2026-W12
Runbook: Update incident runbook with a ‘scale-down-inhibit’ play and include exact commands and dashboards to check
Post-deploy: Monitor for 72h after rollout with increased alerting thresholds and weekly status check

notes: During the deep-dive we discovered that small-sequence customers have a bimodal arrival pattern that becomes problematic when cohorts are too homogeneous. The sigmoid ramp algorithm discussed trades slightly slower reaction time for significantly fewer false positives; stakeholders prefer this trade given SLA risk.
